docs.title: mobsec — an Android pentest rig that actually works
docs.text:
A rooted Android 16 emulator on this laptop, wired end to end: HTTPS decrypted, Frida attached from the first instruction, root hidden, and hardware-backed key attestation spoofed well enough that a real bank-grade server accepts the login.

Everything here runs locally. No cloud, no extra hardware, ~20 GB of disk.

Authorised testing only

The attestation layer makes this device claim to be a different physical phone, and the keybox in use is not ours. Use it against apps you are permitted to test. Nothing in this rig is anonymous: traffic goes out from your own IP.

docs.title: The one-paragraph mental model
docs.text: The emulator boots a Magisk-patched ramdisk, so su works from the first second. Magisk loads three Zygisk modules that matter: TrickyStore fakes the hardware keystore's attestation chain for packages listed in target.txt, PlayIntegrityFix tries (and fails, on an emulator) to satisfy Play Integrity, and Zygisk Next does the injecting in anonymous memory. Cert-Fixer bind-mounts our mitmproxy CA into every process's trust store, including system ones. frida-server runs renamed as hluda under a small custom module, listening on loopback only. On the host, nettap keeps mitmproxy and the adb reverse tunnel alive, fspawn starts an app under Frida with a chosen script profile, and replay re-issues anything you captured.

docs.title: 1. Emulator
docs.text:
pentest16 is a Play Store (google_apis_playstore) system image for API 36, x86_64, pixel_7 profile, 6 GB RAM, 16 GB data partition. Play Store matters: several attestation-ish code paths check for GMS presence and behave differently without it.

It runs with KVM acceleration (/dev/kvm, user in kvm group), 4 vCPUs, and GPU on. Boot from cold is ~90 s; from a snapshot, ~25 s.

docs.title: 2. Root — rootAVD + Magisk
docs.text:
rootAVD patches ramdisk.img of the system image (not the AVD) with Magisk, then the Magisk app does a second "additional setup" pass on first boot. Result: su works, context=u:r:magisk:s0.

Magisk 31.1 specifics that bite:

  • Built-in Zygisk must be off (magisk --sqlite "replace into settings (key,value) values('zygisk',0)") because Zygisk Next owns injection.
  • Magisk's denylist is empty by design here. Adding an app would strip our modules (TrickyStore, PIF) from exactly the app that needs them.
  • magisk --denylist rm <pkg> <process> (two args) segfaults the daemon. Use one argument.

docs.title: 3. Zygisk modules
docs.text:
Module id Job Zygisk Next 1.5.3 zygisksu The injector. zygiskd CLI controls policy, memory type, module list. TrickyStore 1.4.1 tricky_store Replaces the keystore's attestation certificate chain for packages in target.txt using keybox.xml. PlayIntegrityFix 4.9 playintegrityfix Tries to satisfy Play Integrity. On an emulator: NO_INTEGRITY, permanently. HMA-OSS (Vector-flavoured) hma_oss_zygisk Hides other installed packages from a target app (root/emulator detector enumeration). Cert-Fixer 1.1 cert-fixer Bind-mounts user CAs into /apex/com.android.conscrypt/cacerts at post-fs-data, so GMS and Play Store trust mitmproxy too. fsrv (ours) fsrv Renames and autostarts frida-server as /data/adb/fsrv/hluda, loopback only.

Zygisk Next's memory type is set to anonymous so module libs never appear in /proc/<pid>/maps as files.

docs.title: 4. Interception
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant App
    participant Proxy as mitmdump :18080
    participant Up as upstream
    App->>Proxy: HTTP/2 CONNECT (adb reverse tunnel)
    Proxy->>Up: TLS to real server
    Note over Proxy: dump.py writes /tmp/mtflows/<HHMMSS>_<host>_<path>.txt
    Proxy-->>App: TLS with mitmproxy CA
    Note over App: CA trusted because Cert-Fixer mounted it into conscrypt

Two details make this painless:

  • adb reverse (device → host), not a proxy on the LAN, so no http_proxy is needed for pinned apps. adb reverse dies on every reboot; nettap on restores it.
  • Cert-Fixer mounts the CA at boot for the whole system, which is why Play Store and GMS traffic decrypts instead of failing with does not trust the proxy's certificate.

docs.title: 5. Host tooling
docs.text: pentestctl (health), nettap (proxy+tunnel+addon), fspawn (spawn under Frida with a profile), fdp/cdp (WebView DevTools), session (harvest cookies+storage), replay (re-issue requests), recon (static APK), snap (AVD snapshots), uitap (UI automation), asu (run root snippets).

docs.title: What fails if you remove a layer
docs.text: Remove Symptom Cert-Fixer Chrome/WebView still decrypts (user CA), but Play Store and GMS throw TLS handshake errors. TrickyStore target.txt entry App gets the emulator's fake AOSP chain → server rejects with an attestation error. Valid keybox Chain becomes the bundled software AOSP keybox (expired intermediate) → server rejects. zygiskd enforce-denylist off Nothing breaks; denylist simply stops being honoured. adb reverse App talks to a dead proxy: spinner forever, zero flows. This is the #1 "it broke overnight" cause. Zygisk Next No TrickyStore, no PIF, no HMA — attestation spoof and hiding both vanish.

docs.title: Design decisions worth knowing
docs.text:
• Play Store image over AOSP — closer to a real device for attestation checks; the cost is a heavier boot and GMS noise in every capture (filtered by IGNORE in dump.py).
  • Denylist policy default, not whitelist — whitelist mode injects only for listed packages, but WebView renderer sandbox processes (…:sandboxed_process0, isolated uid) never match the package name, so every page load failed with net_error -202. Tried it, reverted it; see Root hiding.
  • frida-server, not gadget — gadget needs per-APK patching and re-signing, which changes the APK signature (and some servers check it). Server-side injection leaves the APK untouched.
  • Loopback-only frida — LISTEN=127.0.0.1:27042 + adb forwarding. Nothing on the LAN can reach the agent, and no frida-server string appears in a listening-socket scan.

docs.title: Attestation & keyboxes
docs.text:
This is the part that usually makes people give up on emulator-based testing. A modern app asks the Android keystore to generate a key with a server-chosen challenge, and the keystore returns a certificate chain signed by Google's servers describing the device. The app ships that chain to its backend, which decides whether to let you in.

On an emulator that chain says "Droid Unregistered Device CA, Google Test LLC" — an obvious emulator. On a real phone it says "hardware-backed, verified boot green, your device". Even with a software keybox the chain is signed by an expired AOSP intermediate. Both get rejected.

sequenceDiagram
    participant App
    participant KS as Android Keystore
    participant TS as TrickyStore (Zygisk)
    participant Srv as Backend
    App->>KS: generateKey(alias, attestationChallenge)
    KS->>TS: real chain (or AOSP fake chain)
    TS-->>App: substituted chain from keybox.xml
    App->>Srv: POST /login { attestation: { chain: [...] } }
    Srv->>Srv: verify chain against Google roots + revocation list
    Srv-->>App: 2000 (accepted) or 4202 (ATTESTATION_UNSUPPORTED)

docs.title: TrickyStore
docs.text:
• Module id tricky_store, manager UI in com.example.target-style apps is not needed — it is driven by two files.
  • target.txt — one package per line: only these apps get spoofed chains.
  • keybox.xml — the replacement chain material (EC and/or RSA), plus the private keys that let the keystore actually sign with it.
  • Reads tee_status; on an emulator teeBroken=true is expected.
adb shell su -c 'cat /data/adb/tricky_store/target.txt'
adb shell su -c 'grep -o "DeviceID=\"[^\"]*\"" /data/adb/tricky_store/keybox.xml'

DeviceID is cosmetic — do not read identity into it

The DeviceID attribute is just a label the upstream keybox author typed. For the public RED-TEAM-KEYBOX source it is literally a Telegram advert (DeviceID="RKP keybox. Join my group: t.me/redteamchannell"). TrickyStore never uses it and the server validates the chain, not the label — so it is normal for it to look like spam and to change on every keybox-refresh. pentestctl status prints it tagged (cosmetic upstream label).

Forgetting target.txt looks like a broken keybox

Before adding the package, the app still receives the emulator's own fake chain. The server says "this device could not be verified" and you blame the keybox. Add the package, force-stop the app, relaunch — no reboot required.

docs.title: Keybox lifecycle
docs.text:
A usable keybox must satisfy all of:

  1. Chain signatures verify up to a known root.
  2. Nothing in the chain is expired.
  3. The serial numbers are not on Google's revocation list (https://android.googleapis.com/attestation/status).
  4. It is a hardware/RKP chain — the server can tell software chains apart, and they are rejected by anything modern.

Check all four before installing:

kbcheck.py --summary /tmp/kb.xml
# SUMMARY device=<cosmetic upstream label> alg=ecdsa len=4 root=None sig=ok leaf_not_after=2026-12-04 revoked=- expired=-
kbcheck.py --strict /tmp/kb.xml      # exit 1 unless every check passes

root=None is normal: the bundled root bundle (tools/keybox-res/) predates the RKP root (CN=Key Attestation CA1), so the root pin cannot be matched — signatures and revocation still validate, and the server is the real judge.

docs.title: The one that works right now
docs.text:
setup-keybox.sh                       # fetch from upstream, validate, install, back up the old one
keybox-refresh                        # same thing, but only if it is actually needed
pentestctl status | grep keybox
#   --   keybox DeviceID="RKP keybox. Join my group: t.me/redteamchannell" (cosmetic upstream label, not an identity — the chain is what matters)
#   ok   keybox leaf valid until 2026-12-04 (8d left)

Source: redteam-git/RED-TEAM-KEYBOX publishes a base64 blob at …/main/conf (refreshed every 4 h upstream). setup-keybox.sh --file <xml> installs a local file; --check validates only.

docs.title: Keeping it alive: keybox-refresh
docs.text:
Keyboxes die quietly — the leaf expires and the server starts answering 4202 again with no other symptom. keybox-refresh is the boring fix:

keybox-refresh                 # refresh only if < 7 days left, revoked, or already expired
keybox-refresh --force         # refresh now, e.g. when the target starts refusing you
keybox-refresh --min-days 20   # keep a wider safety margin
keybox-refresh --dry-run       # validate the device keybox and print what it would do

How it behaves:

  1. Reads the device keybox, runs kbcheck.py --summary (device=… leaf_not_after=… sig=… revoked=…).
  2. Stays put unless the keybox is close to expiry or already dead.
  3. Tries sources in order — redteam, then yuri — accepting only payloads that kbcheck.py --strict accepts (signatures, chain, expiry, of the revocation list).
  4. Backs up the old keybox as keybox.xml.bak_<ts> and force-stops com.example.target, com.android.vending, com.google.android.gms so they re-open the keystore.
  5. Appends to ~/.mobsec/keybox.log.

It runs automatically through a systemd user timer (mobsec-keybox.timer: 10 min after boot, then daily with a randomised delay, Persistent=true):

systemctl --user list-timers | grep mobsec
systemctl --user start mobsec-keybox.service    # run it now
journalctl --user -u mobsec-keybox.service -n 20

The current leaf expires 2026-12-04; pentestctl status prints the remaining days on every run, so the timer is a safety net and not the primary signal.

docs.title: Anatomy of a rejected keybox (real example)
docs.text: The well-known Yurikey keybox had a perfect hardware chain — and its leaf serial bb0d83fa2a47a1ae54c8c359778aaf35 was on Google's revocation list (2222 entries). Everything looked right in the UI, and the server still said no. Always check revocation, not just expiry.

docs.title: What the server actually validates
docs.text:
From the target app's behaviour, in order of strictness:

  1. Chain parses and every signature verifies.
  2. Leaf public key matches the challenge-signed data.
  3. Chain contains Google's RKP attestation extension (hardware root of trust).
  4. No serial is revoked, nothing expired.
  5. Sometimes: verifiedBootState = green, deviceLocked = true, osVersion sane.

TrickyStore supplies 1–5 for keystore users, but the revocation list is checked server-side and cannot be spoofed locally. That is why a revoked keybox is worthless even though the UI shows a beautiful chain.

docs.title: Verifying on-device
docs.text:
Install KeyAttestation (io.github.vvb2060.keyattestation, in apks/) and generate a key:

  • ✅ expected: CN=App Attest Key issued by O=TEE,CN=<32 hex>, "Bootloader is locked", manufacturer from the keybox, ~32 certs issued in the last 30 days.
  • ⚠️ expected on this rig: banner "Unknown root certificate — root is not a known trusted CA". Its local root pool does not contain the RKP root; the target server's does. Not a failure.
  • ❌ if you see CN=Android Keystore Software Attestation Intermediate: target.txt is missing the package, or keybox.xml is the bundled software one.

docs.title: Play Integrity is a different problem
docs.text:
Play Integrity's MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY cannot be faked on an emulator; measured here as UNEVALUATED (Google declines to grade an emulator with no account) before and after PlayIntegrityFix. This rig does not solve PI, and does not need to for apps that use raw key attestation. The mechanics, the integrity tool and the escape routes are on the Play Integrity page.

x86_64 gotcha

PlayIntegrityFork v19 ships only arm64/armv7 zygisk libs, so on this x86_64 image it silently never loads (zygiskd status stops listing playintegrityfix). The installed module is PlayIntegrityFix_v4.9-inject-s.zip, which does ship x86_64. v19 is parked in modules/archive/.

docs.title: Pentest checklist (mapped to this rig)
docs.text:
This is the HackTricks/OWASP-MASTG Android checklist, rewritten as "which command in this rig does that, and where does it stop working". Use it so you do not reinvent steps — and so you do not claim coverage the emulator cannot give you.

Legend: ✔ a command does it · ~ partial, read the note · ✘ impossible or pointless here.

docs.title: 1. Before you install anything (static)
docs.text: Check Command What is it, who signed it, which SDKs recon app.apk ✔ Obfuscation / packer / anti-VM hints recon → Packers section (apkid) ✔ APKiD says anti_vm / anti_debug verify by hand in jadx — it fires on Google/Firebase/Material library code ~ Secrets, API keys, endpoints in DEX/resources recon --deep, then apkleaks section ✔ Rule-based SAST (Weak crypto, WebView, backup flags…) recon → mobsfscan ✔ Manifest triage: exported components, deep links, allowBackup, dataExtractionRules, networkSecurityConfig, usesCleartextTraffic, debuggable recon (summary) + entry (attack sheet) ✔ App Links / assetlinks.json entry → "App links on this device" ✔ Native libs + CVEs apkanalyzer apk summary, unzip -l; CVE mapping by hand ~ Cross-platform framework (Flutter/RN/Tauri/Cordova) find lib/ -name '*.so'; Tauri = libapp_lib.so + remote web UI ✔ Decompile for source review jadx-gui app.apk (or apktool d) ✔ Sideloaded/store differences compare APKs from Play vs vendor — Play App Signing changes the signing key ~

docs.title: 2. Install and get it running
docs.text: Check Command Get past root/emulator detection fspawn <pkg> intercept (HTTP Toolkit set: root detection off, pinning off, proxy overridden) ✔ Get past key attestation setup-keybox.sh / keybox-refresh, target listed in /data/adb/tricky_store/target.txt ✔ Get past Play Integrity see Play Integrity — not passable on an emulator ✘ Force the app to talk to you nettap on (proxy + reverse + addon), then use the app ✔ Launch an exported activity/service/receiver entry <pkg> --run ✔ See what it does with a URL entry <pkg> --only links ✔

docs.title: 3. Runtime: storage
docs.text: Check Command Private dir, sqlite, prefs, webview store pull-data <pkg> (--sql, --grep) ✔ What is actually in the databases sqlite3 ~/.mobsec/data/<pkg>/…/foo.db .dump ✔ Session/refresh tokens at rest pull-data --grep token → then decrypt by hand if needed ✔ Keystore-backed keys fspawn <pkg> attest (20-keystore.js dumps subject/issuer of generated chains) ✔ "Keystore is hardware-backed" claim KeyAttestation app → see Attestation ✔ adb backup extraction blocked on API 31+ unless the app opts in; use pull-data instead ~ External storage / shared prefs pull-data also pulls /sdcard/Android/data/<pkg> ✔

docs.title: 4. Runtime: network
docs.text: Check Command Full request set, decrypted nettap on + flows (files in /tmp/mtflows, index in _index.jsonl) ✔ Pinning fspawn <pkg> intercept ✔ Proxy-unaware / native traffic same profile (in-process proxy override) ✔ WebSocket / GraphQL over WS flows capture the handshake; cdp watch shows app-side messages ~ Edit and re-send a request replay --grep PATH --patch 'field=value' ✔ IDOR / authz testing snap list → clone the AVD, log in as user B (ANDROID_SERIAL), replay user A's requests ~ MQTT/gRPC/QUIC/bluetooth nothing here terminates those; check the app's protocol first ✘

docs.title: 5. Runtime: WebView / hybrid apps
docs.text: Check Command DOM, localStorage, sessionStorage, cookies fdp then cdp eval 'location.href' / session harvest ✔ Console + network of the web layer cdp watch 30 ✔ addJavascriptInterface bridges fspawn <pkg> web shows console; grep the bundle for the bridge name ~ Client-side authz enforced in JS read the bundle: grep -o 'plugin:[^"]*' *.js finds Tauri/Electron IPC commands ✔ Deep links into the web layer entry + cdp eval 'location.href="/route"' ✔

docs.title: 6. Runtime: components and injection
docs.text: Check Command Exported components reachable, permission NOT enforced entry <pkg> --run, watch logcat ✔ Content provider data leak entry provider lines (content query --uri …) — note exported=false + grantUriPermissions=true needs a grant ~ Task hijacking / StrandHogg needs a real launcher and a second malicious app — out of scope for this rig ✘ Tapjacking / overlay attacks needs overlay permissions and a real UI; emulator OK but no template here ✘ Dynamic instrumentation fspawn <pkg> trace|attest|web|spy ✔ Root/emulator checks firing fspawn <pkg> trace → 30-rootcheck.js prints each path/API queried ✔

docs.title: 7. Server side (where the money usually is)
docs.text: Check Command Endpoint inventory flows index + recon --deep endpoints, diffed ✔ Authz: object ownership replay with another user's ids ✔ Mass assignment / field injection replay --patch ✔ Rate limits / lockout replay in a loop, watch status codes ✔ MFA weaknesses session harvest → inspect /auth/session-style endpoints for seeds/tokens ✔ Logout / session invalidation replay the logout, then reuse the cookie ✔

docs.title: 8. What this rig cannot tell you
docs.text:
• Anything hardware-backed that you did not spoof: sensors, Secure Element, StrongBox, real TEE behaviour.
  • Play Integrity verdicts (why).
  • Bluetooth, NFC, USB, SIM/telephony behaviour.
  • OEM-specific bugs (the emulator is AOSP + Google image, no vendor blobs).
  • Performance/timing side channels that depend on real CPU and memory pressure.
  • Whether a leaked key matters — that is a server-side validation question, and the answer changes per target.

docs.title: Reporting habit
docs.text: For every finding, keep the evidence triple: the flow file (/tmp/mtflows/…txt), the replay command that reproduces it, and the app state (which snap image, which user, which Frida profile). _index.jsonl plus a one-line replay command is the cheapest possible repro packet.

docs.title: Captured flows & replay
docs.text: Every interesting request on the device ends up as a file in /tmp/mtflows (change with FLOWDIR). Those files are the raw material for everything else: analysis, replay, fuzzing, evidence.

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
One file per flow, named <HHMMSS>_<host>_<path>.txt:

POST https://crmbff.example.com/auth/mobile/login

--REQ HEADERS--
Headers[(b'content-type', b'application/json'), (b'cookie', b'mtpo.crm=…'), …]

--REQ BODY--
{"userName":"…","password":"…","attestation":{"chain":[ … ]}}

--RESP 200--
Headers[(b'content-type', b'application/json'), …]

--RESP BODY--
{"code":2000,"data":{…}}

Notes:

  • The headers block is mitmproxy's Headers repr on one line — parse with ast.literal_eval after stripping the Headers prefix (that is what replay does).
  • Bodies are truncated at MAXBODY (20 000 bytes) but the index records the real lengths.
  • Two hosts with the same path no longer collide: the host is part of the name, and a -2/-3 suffix is added if the same second produces the same host+path.
  • Names carry no date (only HHMMSS), so never sort flows by name across days — session, replay and snap sort by mtime.

docs.title: The index
docs.text:
tail -3 /tmp/mtflows/_index.jsonl

{"ts": 1795530833, "file": "200353_example_com__.txt", "host": "example.com", "method": "GET", "path": "/s.js", "status": 200, "req_len": 0, "resp_len": 1379}

Quick analysis:

# API surface, most frequent first
jq -r '"\(.method) \(.host)\(.path)"' /tmp/mtflows/_index.jsonl | sed 's/[0-9a-f]\{8,\}/<id>/g' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -30

# errors only
jq -r 'select(.status >= 400) | "\(.status) \(.method) \(.host)\(.path)"' /tmp/mtflows/_index.jsonl | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

# what got sent where with a body
jq -r 'select(.req_len > 0) | "\(.req_len) \(.method) \(.host)\(.path)"' /tmp/mtflows/_index.jsonl | sort -rn | head

docs.title: Replay
docs.text:
replay re-issues a captured request from the host, defaulting to exactly what the app sent, with explicit overrides:

replay --grep 'auth/session'                      # newest match
replay --grep 'auth/session' --session            # inject harvested cookie
replay --grep 'auth/session' --dry                # print, do not send
replay --grep 'chat/messages' --patch 'conversationId="<other>"'   # IDOR probe
replay --grep X --remove-header authorization --dry
replay --grep X -x                                # through mitmproxy → new flow

Patch syntax is a small JSONPath: a.b, items[0].id, a.b[2].c. Values are parsed as JSON when possible (42, true, "str"), else kept as strings.

Every --patch run should start with --dry. It prints the method, URL, headers and the first 300 bytes of body — enough to catch a typo before you send something destructive to a production backend.

docs.title: Why this beats Burp here
docs.text:
• Same headers as the app, including device-specific ones and the cookie jar state at capture time.
  • Attestation-friendly: capture the login once, replay everything else; you never need a fresh keystore challenge for non-login endpoints.
  • Evidence-friendly: -x re-sends through mitmproxy, so the attempt lands in the same flow corpus with a timestamp.

docs.title: Token harvesting
docs.text:
session merges the WebView's document.cookie, localStorage and sessionStorage with the newest captured Cookie header (httpOnly cookies are invisible to JS):

session              # writes ~/.mobsec/session/<ts>.json and latest.json
session show
replay --grep 'chat/loadInitialData' --session

Storage layout:

{"cdp": {"url": "…", "cookie": "…", "localStorage": {…}, "sessionStorage": {…}},
 "flow": {"file": "…", "cookie": "…"}}

docs.title: Spotting the interesting things
docs.text:
Patterns worth grepping for in a fresh corpus:

grep -rlE '"(role|isAdmin|permissions)"' /tmp/mtflows/*.txt | head
grep -rl 'secret\|token\|otp\|mfa' /tmp/mtflows/*.txt | head
grep -rhoE '"https?://[^"]+"' /tmp/mtflows/*.txt | sort -u | head -40      # third-party surface
grep -rh 'set-cookie' /tmp/mtflows/*.txt | sort -u | head                  # flags: HttpOnly? Secure? SameSite?

And the classic: compare what a low-privilege account gets versus a high-privilege one for the same endpoint — same request, two cookies, diff the bodies.

docs.title: Frida & instrumentation
docs.text: Frida is not "installed" here, it is wired: the agent autostarts as a Magisk module under a different name, listens on loopback only, and the host side is a set of script profiles that answer specific questions.

docs.title: The device side
docs.text:
Piece Path Binary /data/adb/fsrv/hluda (renamed frida-server, 17.27.5, x86_64) Config /data/adb/fsrv/conf → AUTOSTART=1, LISTEN=127.0.0.1:27042 Control /data/adb/fsrv/ctl start\|stop\|status Module /data/adb/modules/fsrv (starts it from service.sh) 
adb shell su -c '/data/adb/fsrv/ctl status'     # running pid=2180 listen=127.0.0.1:27042
frida-ps -U | head

Renaming matters: the string frida-server and the default port 27042 are what most detectors grep for in /proc/net/tcp, process lists and file paths. hluda is what a heavily-used public build calls itself; on loopback it is also invisible to the LAN.

docs.title: The host side
docs.text:
frida + frida-tools 17.27.5 (pipx), objection available for quick jobs, and these wrappers:

fspawn <pkg> [profile] [frida args…]   # force-stop, spawn under frida with a script set
fdp [pkg] [port]                       # discover webview_devtools_remote_<pid>, adb forward
cdp url | eval "<js>" | watch [secs]   # Chrome DevTools Protocol client for the WebView
session                                # harvest cookies/localStorage/sessionStorage

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text: Profile Scripts Use it for trace core, webview-debug, rootcheck, tls first look: what does this app touch, what does it check web core, webview-debug WebView/Tauri/Cordova apps — enables CDP attest core, keystore key generation, attestation challenge, chain dump spy core, webview-debug + 3 Medusa modules anti-root bypass, OkHttp logging, SQLite queries intercept 9 HTTP Toolkit scripts pinning bypass + proxy override + CA injection + root-detect off full everything local kitchen sink; expect noise raw none isolate whether a script is the problem

docs.title: The local script set
docs.text:
File What it hooks 00-core.js logging helpers on globalThis, process/arch info, a filtered exception handler (only reports faults in app-owned libs, capped at 5 — Frida 17 removed global; use globalThis) 05-webview-debug.js WebView.setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled(true), console messages, URL loads 10-jni.js scans loaded classes for tauri/plugin classes, wraps methods, lists libapp_lib.so symbols matching permanent_login|attest|secure_storage|plugin 20-keystore.js KeyGenParameterSpec.setAttestationChallenge / setIsStrongBoxBacked, KeyStore.getCertificateChain subject/issuer dump 30-rootcheck.js File.exists/canRead/canExecute/isFile/isDirectory on su/magisk/frida/xposed paths, Runtime.exec, getPackageInfo, Debug.isDebuggerConnected, Build fields 40-tls.js SSLContext.init trust managers, NetworkSecurityPolicy; --bypass = trust-all 
# with extra args, everything after the profile is passed to frida
fspawn com.example.app trace --runtime=v8
fspawn com.example.app raw -l ~/my-script.js

docs.title: Background runs
docs.text:
Frida's REPL needs a tty. frida -U -f pkg < /dev/null exits immediately, and pkill -f 'frida -U -f pkg' can kill the shell that issued it. Use a fifo:

mkfifo /tmp/f; sleep 900 > /tmp/f &
fspawn com.example.app intercept < /tmp/f > /tmp/frida.log 2>&1 &
tail -f /tmp/frida.log

docs.title: WebView = CDP
docs.text:
For hybrid apps this is the highest-value tool in the rig: no hooks, full DOM, console, network view and storage.

fspawn com.example.app web
fdp com.example.app          # pid=9918 socket=webview_devtools_remote_9918 -> http://127.0.0.1:9222
cdp url                      # {"id":…, "url":"https://app.example.com/chat", "title":"App"}
cdp eval "JSON.stringify(Object.keys(localStorage))"
cdp eval "document.cookie"
cdp watch 15                 # stream console + network events for 15 s

session uses the same channel to merge document.cookie, localStorage and sessionStorage with the newest captured cookie header (httpOnly cookies never show up in JS).

docs.title: Stolen modules (Medusa)
docs.text:
tools/medusa is a vendored copy; bin/medusa-export converts its JSON modules into standalone JS:

medusa-export list
medusa-export export --set core      # writes frida/medusa/*.js
medusa-export export http_communications__okhttp3_retrofit

Medusa's modules assume the framework's helpers (colorLog, Module.findExportByName). The exporter injects a shim: Color, colorLog, Options defaults, __mod('libc.so', …), plus Frida-17 polyfills for Module.findExportByName / getExportByName.

file_system__shared_preferences crashes WebView apps

It replaces getSharedPreferences() globally and Chromium then dies with NullPointerException: … SharedPreferences$Editor.apply() on a null object reference. Keep it out of profiles for any app with a WebView; load it by hand only for native-only apps.

docs.title: When Frida itself is the problem
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Failed to spawn: unable to find process package not installed / wrong user adb shell pm list packages \| grep name spawns then instantly detaches script threw at load run profile raw, then add scripts one by one access-violation spam the exception handler reporting ART's own SIGSEGVs already filtered in 00-core.js; check the PC is in an app lib frida-ps hangs server died (OOM, or killed by a detector) /data/adb/fsrv/ctl start

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
adb reverse — forwards a port on the device to the host. Used so the app can reach mitmproxy on 127.0.0.1:18080 without a LAN proxy. Dies on every reboot.

Attestation chain — certificate chain returned by the Android keystore for a generated key: leaf (app key) → TEE intermediate → Droid CA → Google root. Encodes device identity, lock state and verified-boot status.

AVD — Android Virtual Device. Here: pentest16, pixel_7 profile, API 36 Play Store image.

Bootloader locked / verified boot — properties the server can read from the attestation extension. TrickyStore's keybox decides what the server sees.

CDP — Chrome DevTools Protocol. Over adb forward :9222 it gives DOM, console, storage and network for any debuggable WebView.

Cert-Fixer — Magisk module that bind-mounts user CAs into /apex/com.android.conscrypt/cacerts at post-fs-data, so system apps (GMS, Play Store) trust mitmproxy.

conscrypt — Android's TLS provider and the place the system trust store lives since Android 14 (moved out of /system/etc/security/cacerts).

denylist (Magisk) — packages that get no module injection. Empty in this rig on purpose: TrickyStore/PIF must reach the target app.

denylist policy (Zygisk Next) — default (inject everywhere except denylisted) or whitelist (inject only listed). Whitelist breaks WebView renderer sandboxes.

frida-server — the on-device agent. Here renamed hluda, autostarted by the fsrv Magisk module, listening on loopback only.

gadget — Frida's injectable library for non-rooted devices; requires patching and re-signing the APK, which changes its signature. Not used here.

HMA-OSS — "Hide My Applist" fork: hides installed packages from a target app's enumeration. Installed, hide list empty.

keybox.xml — TrickyStore's replacement cert+key material: EC and/or RSA chains plus private keys. Must be hardware (RKP), unexpired and unrevoked.

keybox revocation list — Google's published serial blacklist at android.googleapis.com/attestation/status. Server-side check; cannot be spoofed locally.

KVM — kernel virtual machine; /dev/kvm + kvm group membership makes the emulator usable.

Magisk — systemless root. Version 31.1 here, applied to the system image's ramdisk via rootAVD.

mitmproxy / mitmdump — the intercepting proxy. mitm/dump.py addon writes one file per flow.

Play Integrity (PI) — Google's app-level integrity API (device/app/account verdicts). Emulator → NO_INTEGRITY; not solvable here.

PIF (PlayIntegrityFix) — module that tries to satisfy PI by spoofing props; on an emulator it still fails.

post-fs-data — earliest Magisk boot stage; where Cert-Fixer mounts CAs.

RKP — Remote Key Provisioning. Modern hardware attestation where keys/certs are provisioned by Google per device.

rootAVD — script that patches an AVD's ramdisk.img with Magisk; modifies the system image, not the AVD config.

snapshot (AVD) — full VM state save/restore (adb emu avd snapshot save). ~5 GB, ~25 s restore.

TrickyStore — Zygisk module that substitutes keystore attestation chains for packages in target.txt using keybox.xml.

TEE — Trusted Execution Environment; hardware side that produces attestation. Emulators fake it (teeBroken=true).

Zygisk — Magisk's code-injection mechanism into zygote-spawned apps. Disabled in Magisk itself here; Zygisk Next provides it.

zygiskd — Zygisk Next's control CLI (status, enforce-denylist, denylist-policy, memory-type).

Zygisk-Assistant — popular root-hiding module. Not used: it requires targets in Magisk's denylist, which strips our spoofing modules from those same apps.

docs.title: Play Integrity (the other attestation)
docs.text:
Two different things get called "attestation" in Android pentests, and confusing them wastes days:

What it proves Who checks it Can this rig fake it? Key attestation (Android Keystore / RKP) "this key lives in a TEE on a device whose boot state is X" your target's backend, per-request Yes — TrickyStore + keybox, see Attestation Play Integrity (IntegrityManager.requestIntegrityToken) "this APK, installed from Play, on a Google-approved device, right now" Google evaluates, your backend reads the verdict JSON No, not on an emulator

Play Integrity is Google's own server-side verdict. You cannot compute it locally, and the request only works for a Play-distributed, Play-signed app with a Play Console project — which is why pentest tooling ships its own checker APK.

docs.title: Measuring it on this rig
docs.text:
integrity          # taps the button in SPIC, scrapes the verdict JSON from logcat
integrity --json          # raw verdict

integrity drives SPIC (com.henrikherzig.playintegritychecker, in apks/): force-stops it, launches it, finds the "Make Play Integrity Request" button via uiautomator dump, taps it, and parses the JSON block SPIC prints to I/System.out (that is where the library dumps the token payload).

Measured on this AVD, twice, before and after PlayIntegrityFix:

package           : com.henrikherzig.playintegritychecker
app recognition   : UNEVALUATED
device verdict    : —
recent activity   : UNEVALUATED
app licensing     : UNEVALUATED
play protect      : UNEVALUATED

UNEVALUATED (and a missing deviceRecognitionVerdict) is not an error in the rig. Logcat shows the request itself succeeding:

I/Finsky: Integrity key attestation record generated successfully
I/Integrity: requestIntegrityToken() finished for com.henrikherzig.playintegritychecker

Google receives the request and declines to grade it: the device is an emulator and no Google account is signed in. Both conditions must be satisfied for a verdict to exist at all — and even with an account, a Play Store emulator image still cannot return MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY.

Creating a Google account on the AVD is not worth it

It removes the UNEVALUATED state and replaces it with a clean MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY / no DEVICE result. It does not unlock anything, and it puts a real account on a rooted emulator.

docs.title: The modules, and why they do not help here
docs.text:
• PlayIntegrityFix 4.9 (playintegrityfix) patches device props in GMS's process so DroidGuard is less likely to notice the emulator. It is installed and loading (zygiskd status lists it) — it just cannot manufacture a device verdict that Google refuses to issue.
  • PlayIntegrityFork v19 is parked in modules/archive/: it ships only arm64-v8a and armeabi-v7a Zygisk libs, so on this x86_64 image it silently never loads. Watch for that class of bug with zygiskd status after every module change — the module staying absent from modules64: is the tell.
  • TrickyStore fakes the keystore chain. Play Integrity's STRONG_INTEGRITY needs a hardware-backed signature over the app signing key by a Google-trusted root — key attestation spoofing gets you partway, then Google's own evaluation of the resulting record is the wall.
  • TEESimulator (JingMatrix, GPL-3.0) is the current community answer: a software KeyMint that needs a keybox, designed for exactly this "make a non-device look like a device" problem. It is a candidate upgrade for this rig; it is not installed, and it would still be fighting Play's verdict rather than key attestation.

docs.title: When your target actually gates on Play Integrity
docs.text:
In order of cost:

  1. Check it is really PI. If the app also sends a key-attestation chain (Tauri/Rust/native apps often do), the keybox path already covers you — Target is exactly this case.
  2. Frida-hook the client side. IntegrityManager.requestIntegrityToken / the verdict parser in the app: hook the callback and hand back a verdict the app likes. Works only when the backend trusts the client to inspect the verdict, which is a bug worth reporting in itself.
  3. Replay with a good token. session + replay let you re-issue the request with a token minted on a clean device — that is the same thing a real attacker does, and it demonstrates the missing server-side binding.
  4. Use a physical device. No emulator configuration passes MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY; that is the point of the product.

docs.title: Related traps
docs.text:
integrity needs the screen awake and unlocked

uiautomator dump returns nothing useful on a locked screen, and the tap lands nowhere. adb shell input keyevent KEYCODE_WAKEUP first if the AVD has been idle.

SPIC's JSON block ends at an unindented }

The verdict is a multi-line pretty-printed document in logcat. Closing braces of nested objects are indented; only the final one is flush left. Any scraper that stops at the first } truncates the JSON and reports "no verdict" — a bug that cost an hour here.

docs.title: HTTPS interception
docs.text: The goal is boring reliability: every app on the device, including Play Store and GMS, decrypts through mitmproxy, and apps that pin certificates still connect.

docs.title: The chain
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[app] -->|CONNECT :18080| B[adb reverse tunnel]
    B --> C[mitmdump :18080<br/>mitm/dump.py]
    C --> D[upstream]
    C -->|mitmproxy CA| A
    E[Cert-Fixer<br/>post-fs-data] -.->|bind-mount CA| F[/apex/…/conscrypt/cacerts/]
    F -.->|trust store| A
  1. adb reverse tcp:18080 tcp:18080 — device port 18080 is the host's mitmdump. Survives nothing; re-established by nettap on.
  2. Global proxy 127.0.0.1:18080 (optional once fspawn intercept is in play).
  3. CA trust — the mitmproxy CA is installed as a user CA (/data/misc/user/0/cacerts-added/<hash>.0) and then mounted into the system trust store by Cert-Fixer at boot.
  4. Capture — mitm/dump.py writes one file per interesting flow.

docs.title: The CA, exactly
docs.text:
# hash used by the Android trust store (old subject hash, not the new one)
openssl x509 -inform PEM -subject_hash_old -in ~/.mitmproxy/mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem | head -1
# c8750f0d

Installed at /data/misc/user/0/cacerts-added/c8750f0d.0; Cert-Fixer copies and bind-mounts it into /apex/com.android.conscrypt/cacerts for every process, and does the same inside PID 1's mount namespace so late-started system services inherit it.

Verify for a specific process:

PID=$(adb shell pidof com.google.android.gms | tr -d '\r')
adb shell su -c "nsenter --mount=/proc/$PID/ns/mnt -- ls /apex/com.android.conscrypt/cacerts | wc -l"   # 150
adb shell su -c "nsenter --mount=/proc/$PID/ns/mnt -- ls /apex/com.android.conscrypt/cacerts/c8750f0d.0"

Why AlwaysTrustUserCerts was not enough

That module only mounts in service.sh, i.e. after GMS and Play Store have already started, so they kept their original trust store and failed with Client TLS handshake failed … does not trust the proxy's certificate for play-fe.googleapis.com. Cert-Fixer hooks post-fs-data instead. It is installed, trustusercerts is disabled via touch /data/adb/modules/trustusercerts/disable.

docs.title: Pinning
docs.text:
Two independent mechanisms, both from HTTP Toolkit's Frida scripts (frida/httptoolkit/), loaded by fspawn <pkg> intercept:

  • android-certificate-unpinning.js — hooks TrustManagerImpl, OkHttp CertificatePinner, X509TrustManager wrappers, Conscrypt and a long list of third-party pinning libraries, and makes them accept anything.
  • android-certificate-unpinning-fallback.js — a second pass that patches classes after they load, for apps that cache their trust managers early.

Plus two scripts that make interception work without a system proxy:

  • android-proxy-override.js — rewrites System.getProperty("http.proxyHost"), ConnectivityManager.getDefaultProxy() and OkHttp's proxy selector.
  • native-connect-hook.js / native-tls-hook.js — LD_PRELOAD-style hooks (connect, getaddrinfo, SSL_*) so native code (Rust/Flutter/Go) also goes through the proxy and trusts our CA.

Proof, reproducible on this device:

fspawn tech.httptoolkit.pinning_demo intercept
# tap "OkHTTP pinned request" → the app reports success, and the flow shows up:
# GET https://rsa8192--untrusted-root.testserver.host/ HTTP/2.0

Without the profile the same button says Failed and no flow appears.

docs.title: What still resists
docs.text: Case Symptom Workaround Certificate transparency enforcement SSL handshake failed inside a pinned library, even with unpinning Not solved here; needs a CT-aware proxy or hooking the CT verifier (--ct hooks in some forks) Mutual TLS with a hardware key login fails at the TLS layer Keys live in TEE; only TrickyStore-style keystore spoofing can help, and only for attestation, not arbitrary mTLS QUIC / HTTP/3 app works, nothing captured Disable QUIC in the app or block UDP 443 on the device; mitmproxy does not proxy QUIC WebSocket over wss decrypted once upgraded mitmproxy captures the upgrade; use the addon's websocket_message hook if you need frames Apps that pin inside a WebView WebAssembly module nothing in Java hooks fires hook the WebView's network stack (fspawn web) or fall back to replay with harvested tokens

docs.title: The addon
docs.text:
cat ~/mobsec/mitm/dump.py
  • FLOWDIR (default /tmp/mtflows), INTEREST (only matching URLs), IGNORE (default drops googleapis/gstatic/ggbn/firebase/app-measurement/crashlytics noise), MAXBODY (20000 bytes per body).
  • Output <HHMMSS>_<host>_<path>.txt, plus _index.log (human) and _index.jsonl (machine).
  • Restart after editing: nettap off && nettap on. mitmproxy does not hot-reload addons.

docs.title: Sanity checks that catch most "interception is broken" reports
docs.text:
pentestctl status | sed -n '/interception/,$p'
curl -s -x 127.0.0.1:18080 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://example.org   # 200
grep -c 'does not trust the proxy' /tmp/mitm.log                                   # want 0 for GMS
ls -t /tmp/mtflows/*.txt | head -3

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: Two paths: the device already exists (this laptop), or you are rebuilding it on a fresh machine.

docs.title: Path A — the device already exists
docs.text:
# 1. health check (start the emulator first if it is not running)
~/Android/Sdk/emulator/emulator -avd pentest16 -no-snapshot -no-boot-anim &
pentestctl status

# 2. repair the two things a reboot always breaks
pentestctl fix

# 3. capture traffic
nettap on
# ... use the app ...
ls -t /tmp/mtflows/*.txt | head

# 4. instrument the app (Frida + pinning bypass + CA injection)
fspawn com.example.app intercept

# 5. WebView console/DOM/storage
fdp com.example.app      # forwards :9222, prints the DevTools target
cdp url                  # what page is loaded
cdp eval "document.title"

Fastest possible daily start

snap load logged-in      # ~25 s instead of ~90 s cold boot
pentestctl fix
snap load restores apps, sessions and cookies exactly as you left them. See Snapshots.

docs.title: Path B — rebuild from zero
docs.text:
The full beginner walkthrough (SDK install, AVD tuning, rootAVD/Magisk UI clicks, module URLs, CA install, verification) lives in GUIDE-from-scratch.md in the repo root (open it directly, it is not part of this site). Short version:

cd ~/mobsec
./bootstrap.sh --sdk        # host deps + SDK + AVD  (needs your sudo password once, for udev)
emulator -avd pentest16 -no-snapshot &
./fetch-deps.sh             # frida-server, jadx, apktool, scrcpy, rootAVD
./rootAVD.sh …              # see GUIDE step 4 — interactive, Magisk UI driven over adb
./install-device.sh         # modules, frida-server, zygisk policy
./setup-keybox.sh           # fetch + validate a keybox, install to TrickyStore
./setup-net.sh              # CA into the system store, proxy + tunnel
pentestctl status

Order matters: install-device.sh reboots the device, setup-net.sh must run after the first boot with modules installed, and setup-keybox.sh last (it validates against the live device's TrickyStore path).

One interactive step cannot be scripted

Magisk's "install → patch image → additional setup → reboot" flow is UI-driven. rootAVD.sh pauses for it; the GUIDE-from-scratch.md section 4 walks the exact taps, and uitap can drive most of them by text.

docs.title: First real verification (5 minutes)
docs.text:
Do not trust a green pentestctl status alone — prove each layer with a request:

Layer Command Expected Interception curl -s -x 127.0.0.1:18080 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' https://example.org 200, plus a new flow file System trust (GMS) open Play Store, check /tmp/mitm.log no does not trust the proxy's certificate Pinning bypass fspawn tech.httptoolkit.pinning_demo intercept → tap "OkHTTP pinned request" label says Success, request appears in flows Frida fspawn com.android.settings web [fspawn] … scripts=2, no exception spam WebView CDP fdp && cdp url the app's page URL Attestation KeyAttestation app → "Attest key" leaf issuer O=TEE,CN=<deviceid>, "Bootloader is locked"

docs.title: Sharing this site
docs.text:
The site is served by MkDocs on the host. By default it listens on loopback only:

docs serve                 # http://127.0.0.1:8000/
docs serve --lan           # http://<this-host-ip>:8000/ — phone, second laptop, whatever
docs status                # what it is bound to, and every URL that answers

Two things have to be true for another device to load it:

  1. It is bound to 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1 (docs serve --lan does that; docs status shows the bind).
  2. The host firewall lets the port in. On a box with ufw enabled the default inbound policy is DROP, so once:
sudo ufw allow 8000/tcp
# narrower: sudo ufw allow from 192.168.0.0/24 to any port 8000 proto tcp

To keep it up permanently (survives logout/reboot, restarts on failure):

systemctl --user enable --now mobsec-docs        # unit in ~/.config/systemd/user/
journalctl --user -u mobsec-docs -f

It is a plain MkDocs site: no auth, no TLS. Anyone on that network can read the whole rig, including which target you are testing — put it behind Tailscale or an SSH tunnel (ssh -L 8000:127.0.0.1:8000 host) if the network is not yours.

docs.text:

docs.title: Rebuild from scratch
docs.text:
Two artefacts describe a rebuild:

  • GUIDE-from-scratch.md — the narrative walkthrough (12 sections, beginner-friendly, includes the interactive Magisk UI steps and every download URL).
  • bootstrap.sh / fetch-deps.sh / install-device.sh / setup-keybox.sh / setup-net.sh — the automated path, in that order.

docs.title: Automated path
docs.text:
git clone <your copy> ~/mobsec && cd ~/mobsec

./bootstrap.sh --sdk        # host deps, pipx tools, Android SDK, AVD creation, PATH block
emulator -avd pentest16 -no-snapshot -no-boot-anim &
./fetch-deps.sh             # frida-server (x86_64 + arm64), jadx, apktool, scrcpy, rootAVD
# >>> root the image with rootAVD (interactive, see GUIDE §4) <<<
./install-device.sh         # Magisk modules, frida-server staging, zygisk policy, reboot
./setup-keybox.sh           # fetch + validate + install a keybox
./setup-net.sh              # install mitm CA into the system store, proxy + tunnel
pentestctl status

docs.title: Why the order is fixed
docs.text:
Step Depends on Fails if skipped bootstrap.sh — no SDK/adb/emulator/AVD fetch-deps.sh network nothing to install downstream rootAVD booted, unrooted device install-device.sh aborts on missing su install-device.sh root no TrickyStore/PIF/Cert-Fixer/fsrv setup-keybox.sh TrickyStore on device attestation stays software/AOSP setup-net.sh Cert-Fixer installed + one boot user apps work, GMS/Play Store do not

install-device.sh finishes with a reboot; wait for adb wait-for-device before continuing.

docs.title: What is interactive
docs.text: Only Magisk's first-run flow: Install → Patch firmware/image → Select from storage → fakeboot.img → OK → additional setup → reboot, plus granting su to shell. GUIDE §4 has the exact taps; uitap can drive them by text, but expect to babysit it once.

docs.title: Sharing the rig with a colleague
docs.text:
zip -qr ~/share-zip/mobsec-rig-$(date +%Y%m%d).zip ~/mobsec \
  -x '*/tools/jadx*' '*/tools/scrcpy*' '*/tools/apktool*' '*/tools/frida-server-*' \
     '*/modules/MagiskFrida*' '*/modules/archive/*' '*/apks/*' '*/tools/medusa/.venv/*' \
     '*/site/*' '*/.mobsec/*' '*/__pycache__/*'

Deliberately excluded, with reasons:

Excluded Why keybox.xml, .pem, .p12 key material; the recipient must fetch their own ~/.mobsec/session, ~/.mitmproxy live cookies/tokens and your private CA AVD snapshots 5 GB each, host-specific tool binaries (jadx, scrcpy, frida-server) re-downloadable via fetch-deps.sh, keeps the zip ~25 MB MagiskFrida-*.zip 141 MB, superseded by the fsrv module

The recipient still needs their own adb device and must run setup-net.sh so their mitmproxy CA (not ours) is installed. SHARING.md in the archive carries the exact run order and this table.

docs.title: Verification after a rebuild
docs.text:
pentestctl status                                  # every section green
frida-ps -U | head -3                              # 150+ processes
curl -s -x 127.0.0.1:18080 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://example.org   # 200
fspawn tech.httptoolkit.pinning_demo intercept     # "OkHTTP pinned request - Success"
recon com.android.settings --deep                  # recon sanity check
snap save logged-in                                # your first restore point

docs.title: Version pinning that matters
docs.text:
Component Version Why pinned Magisk 31.1 Zygisk Next expects it; older Magisk has no --sqlite settings write Zygisk Next 1.5.3-880 later builds changed zygiskd flags frida-server 17.27.5 must match host frida exactly; 17.x removed global, changed Module API Frida host 17.27.5 mismatch = "unable to communicate with remote frida-server" PlayIntegrityFix 4.9-inject-s v19 has no x86_64 zygisk lib jadx 1.5.7 apkleaks shells out to it mitmproxy 12.3.1 addon uses http.HTTPFlow API (stable since 9)

When you bump a version, re-run the verification list top to bottom before trusting the rig.

docs.title: Static recon
docs.text: Dynamic testing tells you what the app did; static testing tells you what it can do. recon runs the static pass in one command and produces a report you can read in two minutes.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
recon /path/to/app.apk
recon com.example.app --deep        # pulls base.apk from the device, then decompiles
recon app.apk -o /tmp/out

Output:

~/.mobsec/recon/<pkg>-<timestamp>/
├── report.md            <- read this
├── app.apk
└── raw/
    ├── badging.txt      aapt2 dump badging
    ├── manifest.xml     apkanalyzer manifest print
    ├── apkid.txt        packers / obfuscators / anti-analysis
    ├── apkleaks.json    secrets + endpoints (+ .log)
    ├── mobsfscan.json   SAST rules
    └── endpoints.txt    only with --deep (jadx + grep)

docs.title: What the report contains, and how to read it
Exported components
docs.text: The attack surface that does not require the app to be running. For each component: permission, actions, categories, data (scheme/host/path/mime). Anything exported without a signature-level permission is worth a adb shell am start / am broadcast probe.

docs.title: Packers / anti-analysis (APKiD)
docs.text:
Read this with suspicion. APKiD matches library code too:

Tag Meaning What to do packer: … packer/obfuscator heuristic decide whether to test the packed layer or the loader anti_vm / anti_debug emulator/debugger checks verify by reading the class before believing it compiler: unknown not a real finding ignore

Concrete example from this rig: Target was tagged anti_vm + packer: DexGuard, and every hit turned out to be library code:

  • W0/c.java → Firebase CCT metadata (sdk-version, Build.MODEL, Build.FINGERPRINT)
  • p003a2/v.java → Material MaterialAutoCompleteTextView (a Meizu hint workaround)
  • p045n1/k.java → GMS DialogRedirect logging
  • p019g/A.java → !"robolectric".equals(Build.FINGERPRINT)

So: no app-level emulator check in the DEX. The DexGuard tag was R8 single-letter-package confusion. Ten minutes of reading beat a day of chasing a phantom.

docs.title: Secrets / endpoints (apkleaks)
docs.text:
Categories with hit counts. Triage rules:

  • Google_API_Key / Firebase keys are usually not secrets — they are restricted by package name + SHA-1. Report only if a restriction test shows otherwise.
  • Random 30–40 char strings tagged Artifactory_Password are frequently obfuscation noise; grep the decompiled tree for the value before writing a finding.
  • Version strings (1.0.0.2) match IP_Address; ignore.
  • Real finds look like: hardcoded bearer tokens, private endpoints, staging hosts, cloud storage buckets.

docs.title: SAST (mobsfscan)
docs.text: Rule-based Android checks (exported components, weak crypto, WebView settings, backup flags…). Fast, noisy, useful as a checklist. Zero findings is a valid result — not proof of safety.

docs.title: Deep mode
docs.text: --deep decompiles with jadx (1.5.7) and greps string literals for URLs, then writes endpoints.txt. Use it to build the API list before you even launch the app; combine with the captured flows later.

docs.title: A realistic order of operations
docs.text:
1. recon com.example.app --deep — components, permissions, endpoints, secrets.
  2. Note the exported components and any endpoint that looks internal (/admin, /internal, versioned staging hosts).
  3. Launch with fspawn com.example.app web (or intercept) and capture the real request set.
  4. Diff static endpoints vs captured endpoints: what the app can call but did not is where the interesting bugs live.
  5. Only then start replay fuzzing.

docs.title: Extending it
docs.text:
recon is a shell script; every step is independent (aapt2, apkanalyzer, apkid, apkleaks, mobsfscan, jadx). Add steps by copying the pattern in ~/mobsec/bin/recon — each writes into raw/ and appends a section to report.md.

Useful manual follow-ups it does not do:

# who signs it / is it debuggable
apksigner verify --print-certs app.apk
aapt2 dump xmltree app.apk --file AndroidManifest.xml | grep -i debuggable

# backend fingerprinting from the flows
jq -r 'select(.status>=400) | "\(.status) \(.method) \(.host)\(.path)"' /tmp/mtflows/_index.jsonl | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

docs.title: Snapshots
docs.text: A cold boot costs ~90 seconds plus a login. A snapshot restore costs ~25 seconds and comes back to whatever state was saved — including a logged-in app, if that is what you froze.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
snap list                 # name, size, timestamp of newest file
snap save                 # save as 'logged-in' (default)
snap save before-fuzz     # named
snap load                 # restore 'logged-in'
snap load before-fuzz
snap rm before-fuzz
snap boot                 # cold boot, no snapshot

Under the hood:

adb emu avd snapshot save logged-in
emulator -avd pentest16 -snapshot logged-in -no-snapshot-save -no-boot-anim

-no-snapshot-save is deliberate: when the emulator exits it would otherwise overwrite the snapshot with whatever half-broken state you were in.

docs.title: What survives a restore
docs.text:
Survives Does not survive installed apps and their data adb reverse tunnel (host-side) logged-in sessions/cookies in app storage mitmdump process (host-side) Magisk modules + mount state sometimes frida-server (pentestctl fix restarts it) keybox, target.txt global proxy setting? (survives, but points at a dead tunnel)

That is why the documented restore sequence is:

snap load logged-in
pentestctl fix          # re-establishes reverse + frida
pentestctl status

docs.title: When a snapshot is a trap
docs.text:
Snapshots capture mount state, so a snapshot taken while a module was broken keeps restoring the broken mount. Symptoms: Cert-Fixer log says it ran, but GMS still cannot TLS. Fix: cold boot (snap boot), verify, then snap save again under a new name.

Rules:

  • After installing/removing a Magisk module or changing the CA, cold boot once, verify pentestctl status + a GMS request, then save a new snapshot.
  • Keep at most a handful: each is ~5 GB.
  • Name by intent (logged-in, pre-fuzz, clean-no-modules), not by date.
  • A snapshot is only as logged-in as the moment you saved it. After keybox-refresh rotates the keybox, the device presents a new attestation identity on the next launch and the backend drops the session — a snapshot saved before the rotation restores a logged-out app. Re-login (you need the TOTP), then snap save logged-in again.

snap save refuses to work after snap load

load/boot start the emulator with -no-snapshot-save so a broken session cannot overwrite a good snapshot. The emulator reports the refusal as UNSUPPORTED_VK_APP, which looks like a GPU problem and is not. snap save <name> --reopen cold-boots keeping /data, then saves.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text: Action Time Disk cold boot ~90 s — snapshot restore ~21–25 s — one snapshot — ~5.2 GB

docs.text:
adb reverse --list               → host-16 tcp:18080 tcp:18080

If any of those drift, run pentestctl fix and read Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Root hiding
docs.text: Root is required for everything else here, so hiding it is a permanent tax. This rig hides the mechanisms (su binary, Magisk daemon, Zygisk libs, Frida) rather than trying to make a detector believe the device is unmodified — the attestation layer handles the "is this a real phone" question separately.

docs.title: What is hidden, and how
docs.text: Mechanism Visibility Mitigation in this rig su binary / magisk filesystem paths Magisk's own mount/masking; app denylist empty so modules keep working Zygisk injection /proc/<pid>/maps, dlopen paths Zygisk Next memory-type anonymous → no file-backed libs Module mounts /proc/<pid>/mountinfo only whitelisted apps see them (default policy) Frida process name, listening port, string frida-server renamed hluda, loopback only, no default port on LAN Package enumeration getPackageInfo / queryIntentActivities HMA-OSS, scoped per target with hma Attestation keystore chain TrickyStore + keybox (see Attestation)

docs.title: Zygisk Next knobs
docs.text:
/data/adb/modules/zygisksu/bin/zygiskd is the control surface:

zygiskd status
zygiskd enforce-denylist enabled      # honour Magisk's denylist
zygiskd denylist-policy default       # default | whitelist
zygiskd memory-type anonymous         # default | anonymous
zygiskd disable-zygisk false

Current config (survives reboot):

inject_state:1  denylist_policy:0 (default)  enforce_denylist:1  memory_type:1 (anonymous)
modules64: 3,zygisk_vector,hma_oss_zygisk,playintegrityfix

docs.title: The whitelist trap
docs.text:
denylist-policy whitelist means only listed packages get module injection — attractive for stealth, and it breaks WebView apps:

WebView renderer (…:sandboxed_process0, isolated uid u0ai9000) does not match the package name
→ no modules injected → no CA / no unpinning in the sandboxed renderer
→ net_error -202 (SSL handshake failed) on every page

Verified and reverted. Keep default, and keep the app you are testing out of Magisk's denylist.

docs.title: Magisk denylist: keep it empty
docs.text:
adb shell su -c 'magisk --denylist ls'      # expected: empty

If an app is in the denylist, Magisk strips module mounts from it — which is exactly where TrickyStore and PIF need to be. Hiding by denylisting is incompatible with spoofing. Choose one per app.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
magisk --denylist rm <pkg> <process> segfaults the daemon

Two-argument form kills magiskd; afterwards magisk -v says Cannot connect to daemon: Connection refused (os error 111) and su is gone with it. Only a reboot recovers. Always pass a single package argument.

Magisk 31.1 removed 'Hide the Magisk app'

There is no stub-repackaging option in Settings and no CLI equivalent. Package-level hiding is HMA-OSS's job; keep that expectation straight when a detector lists installed packages.

docs.title: HMA-OSS: hiding packages from one app at a time
docs.text: HMA-OSS (hma_oss_zygisk, manager org.frknkrc44.hma_oss) hooks package queries inside a chosen app and filters the answer. It is scoped per target: you say "when this app asks, act as if these packages do not exist".

docs.title: The file that matters
docs.text:
/data/misc/hide_my_applist_bkpzksjqktswmspy/config.json

One JSON document, schema configVersion: 95, with a scope object keyed by target package. Each entry is an AppConfig:

"com.example.target": {
  "useWhitelist": false,
  "excludeSystemApps": true,
  "applyPresets": ["detector_apps","root_apps","shizuku_dhizuku","sus_apps","xposed"],
  "applySettingsPresets": ["accessibility","dev_options"],
  "extraSettings": {"settingsList": []},
  "extraAppList": [], "extraOppositeAppList": []
}

Preset names (they are the module's, not yours): apps = accessibility_apps, custom_rom, detector_apps, root_apps, shizuku_dhizuku, sus_apps, xposed; settings = accessibility, dev_options, input_method. The five app presets above are what you want against a root-detector: Magisk, KeyAttestation, Frida tooling, other test apps, Xposed-era leftovers.

docs.title: Doing it from the host, not the UI
docs.text:
hma show                          # current scope entries
hma hide com.example.target       # 5 app presets + 2 settings presets (defaults)
hma hide com.example.target --presets root_apps,sus_apps --settings dev_options
hma targets                       # what the scope currently names
hma unhide com.example.target     # needs a reboot, see the trap below
hma backup / hma restore          # snapshot the config before experiments

hma writes the config in place over su, so HMA's FileObserver(configFile, CLOSE_WRITE or ATTRIB) picks it up. Logcat then shows (HMA-Service) Config loaded (three times per write — chmod fires ATTRIB as well).

Un-hiding does not take effect until you reboot

HMAServiceDataHolder.shouldHideFromUid() answers from a uidHideCache before it looks at the config, and only the manager-app pipe clears that cache — the file-reload path does not. Measured: hma hide on a live app works immediately (257 → 252 packages, Magisk hidden), hma unhide changes the file and nothing else. Reboot to un-hide.

The manager app only saves on onPause

If you configure HMA in its UI and press Back, nothing is written — AppSettingsV2Fragment persists in onPause. Press HOME (or leave the app) to commit. This is why hand-editing config.json with hma is the less surprising path.

A config.json created after boot is never watched

The FileObserver is constructed at boot even when the file is missing. If HMA has never written a config on this boot, your first hma hide needs one reboot before it has any effect. Check with hma show — if it is empty and you just created a scope, reboot, then re-apply.

docs.title: Verifying hiding actually works
docs.text:
Measure with an app that declares QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES. Without it, Android 11+ package-visibility filtering makes every app look clean:

pm list packages                     → 255 packages
Target getInstalledPackages(0)       → 91     (no QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES)
pinning-demo getInstalledPackages(0) → 90     (no QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES)
ApplistDetector (QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES) → 252/256 and Magisk visible or not

Use apks/ApplistDetector.V2.4.apk (icu.nullptr.applistdetector, Dr-TSNG) as the detector:

asu 'am start -n icu.nullptr.applistdetector/.MainActivity'
# then read its "Installed apps" count and the Magisk/KeyAttestation rows

Measured on this rig, detector scoped, before vs after reboot:

state installed count com.topjohnwu.magisk baseline, no scope 256 visible scoped + reboot 252 hidden live-added scope (Chrome) 257 → 252 visible → hidden, no reboot needed

HMA never hides a target app from itself, so the detector still lists icu.nullptr.applistdetector — that is correct behaviour, not a leak.

Hiding does not disturb spoofing: after HMA was enabled, KeyAttestation still reported the keybox chain (CN=Droid CA2, O=Google LLC) and Bootloader is locked.

# module mounts visible to a normal app vs a module-injected app
adb shell su -c 'wc -l < /proc/<settings-pid>/mountinfo'     # ~157
adb shell su -c 'wc -l < /proc/<target-pid>/mountinfo'       # ~167 (10 module mounts)

# no zygisk/tricky libs mapped
adb shell su -c 'grep -cE "zygisk|tricky" /proc/<target-pid>/maps'   # 0

The 10-mount difference is the honest answer to "is injection scoped": non-target apps see zero module mounts.

docs.title: What this does not hide
docs.text:
• Emulator fingerprints (ro.kernel.qemu, goldfish hardware, sensor set). Apps that check them are dealt with by intercept's root/emulator detection bypass, not by this layer.
  • A keybox that is revoked — that is server-side truth, see Attestation.
  • Your traffic — it leaves from the host's IP through mitmproxy.

docs.title: Command reference
docs.text: Everything is in ~/mobsec/bin (already on PATH). All commands assume the emulator is running.

docs.title: pentestctl
docs.text:
pentestctl status     # device, root, zygisk, attestation (keybox expiry!), frida, interception
pentestctl fix        # nettap on + restart frida-server; repairs reboot damage
Sections and what they read:

Section Source of truth device adb shell getprop root su -c id, su -c magisk -v zygisk zygiskd status attestation /data/adb/tricky_store/{keybox.xml,target.txt} + kbcheck.py frida /data/adb/fsrv/ctl status interception /tmp/mitm.pid, adb reverse --list, settings get global http_proxy, flow count, cert-fixer log

docs.title: nettap
docs.text:
nettap on [port]      # mitmdump (idempotent) + adb reverse + global proxy
nettap off            # kill mitmdump, remove proxy/reverse
nettap status         # proxy, reverse, pid, addon path, flow count
Env: ADDON (dump.py), FLOWDIR, INTEREST, PORT. nettap on refuses to start if the addon or mitmdump is missing instead of dying silently.

docs.title: snap
docs.text:
snap list             # snapshots + size + newest file mtime
snap save [name]      # default 'logged-in'
snap load [name]      # boots with -snapshot -no-snapshot-save (~25 s)
snap rm [name]
snap boot             # cold boot the AVD

docs.title: fspawn <pkg> [profile] [frida args…]
docs.text:
Profiles: trace (default), web, attest, spy, intercept, full, raw. See Frida. 

fspawn com.example.app intercept
fspawn com.example.app raw -l ~/hooks.js

docs.title: fdp [pkg] [port]
docs.text: Finds webview_devtools_remote_<pid> in /proc/net/unix (auto-detects the foreground app when pkg is omitted), forwards :9222, prints the target list.

docs.title: cdp url|eval "<js>"|watch [secs]
docs.text: Minimal CDP client (python3 + websockets). eval awaits promises; watch streams console/network events.

docs.title: session
docs.text:
session            # harvest -> ~/.mobsec/session/<ts>.json + latest.json
session show       # pretty-print
session cookie     # just the Cookie header value
Merges document.cookie, localStorage, sessionStorage from the WebView with the newest flow's cookie header (httpOnly cookies are invisible to JS). TARGET=target session restricts the page match.

docs.title: medusa-export
docs.text:
medusa-export list [filter]
medusa-export export NAME... | --set core|web|dump
medusa-export path NAME

docs.title: replay
docs.text:
replay --grep 'chat/loadInitialData' --session
replay --grep X --patch 'a.b=42' --patch 'items[0].id=1' --dry
replay --grep X --method POST --path /other --body '{"q":"x"}'
replay --grep X --header 'x-test: 1' --remove-header cookie -x --full --save out.json
Defaults to exactly what the app sent (same headers, cookie, body). -x sends through mitmproxy (captured as evidence). --save writes the response body.

docs.title: recon
docs.text:
recon <apk|package> [--deep] [-o DIR]
Writes ~/.mobsec/recon/<pkg>-<ts>/report.md + raw/. See Static recon.

docs.title: entry
docs.text:
Turns the manifest into copy-paste attack commands — one adb shell am start|broadcast|content line per exported component and deep link. 

entry com.example.app                 # attack sheet
entry com.example.app --run            # and fire every probe
entry com.example.app --only links -o /tmp/sheet.txt
The sheet lists exported activities/services/receivers with their required permissions, content providers (including exported=false + grantUriPermissions=true), every scheme://host deep link, and pm get-app-links state.

docs.title: pull-data
docs.text:
The honest replacement for adb backup (blocked on API 31+): root-tars the app's private dir, pulls it, and summarises. 

pull-data com.example.app                 # -> ~/.mobsec/data/<pkg>/
pull-data com.example.app --sql           # + row counts for every sqlite db
pull-data com.example.app --grep token    # grep the pull
pull-data com.example.app --no-pull       # re-summarise only
Reports the biggest files, every SQLite database with tables/row counts, shared_prefs and JSON lines that look like secrets, and pulls /sdcard/Android/data/<pkg> too. Writes summary.txt next to the extracted tree.

docs.title: setup-keybox.sh / keybox-refresh
docs.text:
setup-keybox.sh --check                 # validate the installed keybox only
setup-keybox.sh --file my-keybox.xml    # install a local one
keybox-refresh [--force] [--min-days 7] [--dry-run]
keybox-refresh refreshes automatically only when the leaf is close to expiry or revoked, validates candidates with kbcheck.py --strict, and backs up the old keybox. It is wired to a systemd user timer. See Attestation.

docs.title: hma
docs.text:
Root-hiding scope editor for HMA-OSS (writes config.json over su, reloads live). 

hma show
hma hide com.example.app [--presets root_apps,sus_apps] [--settings dev_options]
hma unhide com.example.app               # takes effect after a reboot
hma backup / hma restore
hma targets / hma presets
Un-hiding needs a reboot (uid cache); a config.json created after boot needs one reboot before it is watched. See Root hiding.

docs.title: integrity
docs.text:
Play Integrity verdict from SPIC, scraped out of logcat. 

integrity     # human-readable verdict
integrity --json     # raw JSON
Expect UNEVALUATED on this AVD — it is Google declining to grade an emulator with no account, not a rig failure. See Play Integrity.

docs.title: asu
docs.text:
Runs a root shell snippet without the adb shell su -c "…" quoting nightmare: 

asu 'for p in /data/adb/modules/*; do echo $p; done'

docs.title: uitap
docs.text:
Text-driven UI automation (uiautomator dump under the hood) — survives layout changes that break fixed coordinates: 

uitap dump
uitap click "Login"
uitap click "^Allow$" --exact
uitap wait "Logged in" --timeout 20

docs.title: apktool
docs.text: Wrapper around the pinned apktool_3.0.3.jar (apktool d app.apk -o out).

docs.title: docs
docs.text:
The documentation site you are reading, served locally. 

docs serve            # mkdocs serve on 127.0.0.1:8000 (background, pid in /tmp/mkdocs.pid)
docs serve --lan      # bind 0.0.0.0 so other machines can read it (needs a firewall rule, see below)
docs build            # mkdocs build --strict
docs status           # running? bound where? which URLs answer? firewall reminder
docs open | docs stop

For permanent LAN sharing there is a user unit, mobsec-docs.service (systemctl --user enable --now mobsec-docs), and sudo ufw allow 8000/tcp once — ufw's default inbound policy is DROP, so a bound port is not a reachable port.

docs.title: Host environment
docs.text:
java -version          # 21 (jadx/apktool/apkanalyzer)
frida --version        # 17.27.5
mitmdump --version     # 12.3.1
apkid / apkleaks / mobsfscan / objection / scrcpy / adb / emulator
